meta.author: bank-team-integrated-3
meta.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Identify the sample space of an experiment
questions.stem: A debate team flips a coin and rolls a die; which set represents the sample space?

options.text: All pairs of coin outcome and die face
Only the coin outcomes heads and tails
Only the die faces one through six
The single outcome heads on six

questions.explanation: The sample space includes every combination of coin and die results. Omitting either component loses outcomes.

questions.stem: A debate team draws one card from a fair deck; are the 52 outcomes equally likely?

options.text: No, face cards are more likely
Yes, a fair deck gives equal chance to each card
No, red cards are more likely
No, only aces are equally likely

questions.explanation: A fair deck gives each card equal probability. Color or rank does not change fairness.

questions.stem: A debate team spinner has P(red)=0.5, P(blue)=0.3, P(green)=0.2. What is P(red or blue)?
questions.explanation: Add disjoint probabilities: 0.5+0.3=0.8. Non-uniform outcomes still add when disjoint.

questions.stem: A debate team chooses 3 members from 10 for a panel where order does not matter; which formula applies?

options.text: Combination C(10,3) because order is irrelevant

questions.explanation: When order does not matter, use combinations. Permutations count ordered arrangements.

questions.stem: A debate team has P(A)=0.4, P(B)=0.5, P(A and B)=0.2. Are A and B independent? Give P(A)P(B).
questions.explanation: P(A)P(B)=0.4*0.5=0.2, which equals P(A and B), so independent. Product equals joint probability.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret the sign and size of r
questions.stem: A debate team sees r=-0.85 between practice hours and errors. What does that indicate?

options.text: No relationship because r is not 1

questions.explanation: r=-0.85 means strong negative linear association. Magnitude near 1 indicates strength.

questions.stem: A debate team notes ice cream sales and drownings correlate; can we conclude ice cream causes drowning?

options.text: No, correlation alone does not imply causation
Yes, if the sample is large enough
No, because drownings cause ice cream sales

questions.explanation: Correlation indicates association, not causation; confounding variables may explain it. Causation needs experiments.

questions.stem: A debate team codes party affiliation as 0 for Independent, 1 for Democrat, 2 for Republican. What is this encoding called?

options.text: Label encoding with arbitrary integer codes

questions.explanation: Assigning integer codes to categories is label encoding; the numbers carry no order meaning here. One-hot would use separate binary columns.

questions.learningObjective: Identify unsupported claims from a sample
questions.stem: A debate team surveys 50 club members and concludes all students nationwide prefer the policy. Find the error.

options.text: The sample size is too small for any conclusion

questions.explanation: The sample represents club members, not all students nationwide, so generalization is unsupported. Scope, not just size, matters.

questions.stem: A debate team's regression assumes errors are independent. Can this assumption be directly verified from the data?

options.text: Yes, by checking the correlation of residuals
No, independence is often assumed not verified

questions.explanation: Independence of errors is usually assumed; data can suggest violations but cannot fully verify it. Assumptions often rest on design.

questions.stem: A debate team tree: P(rain)=0.3, then P(win|rain)=0.6 and P(win|no rain)=0.4. What is P(win and rain)?
questions.explanation: Multiply along branch: 0.3*0.6=0.18. Joint probability follows the path product.

questions.stem: A debate team has P(A)=0.5, P(B)=0.4, P(A and B)=0.2. Compute P(A|B).
questions.explanation: P(A|B)=P(A and B)/P(B)=0.2/0.4=0.5. Condition on B by dividing.

questions.stem: A debate team models 10 independent questions each with success probability 0.7. What distribution applies?
questions.explanation: Fixed n independent trials with constant success probability defines a binomial. Poisson and geometric differ.

questions.stem: A debate team's scores are normal with mean 70 and sd 5. About what percent fall within one sd of the mean?
questions.explanation: The empirical rule gives about 68% within one standard deviation. This is the familiar 68-95-99.7 rule.

questions.topic: Normal distributions and the empirical rule
questions.learningObjective: Estimate tail probability with empirical rule
questions.stem: A debate team's normal scores have mean 50 and sd 10. About what percent are above 70?
questions.explanation: 70 is two sd above mean; upper tail beyond two sd is about 2.5%. Empirical rule upper 2.5% beyond +2sd.

questions.stem: A debate team takes many samples of size 30; what happens to the sample mean distribution?

options.text: It shrinks to a single point
It stays exactly the population shape
It becomes approximately normal by CLT

questions.explanation: By the central limit theorem, sample means approach normality for large n. Population shape matters less.

questions.topic: Type one and type two errors
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish Type I and Type II errors
questions.stem: A debate team rejects a true null hypothesis. Which error is that?

options.text: Type II error, a false negative
Type I error, a false positive
Power error from low sample size
No error because rejection is valid

questions.explanation: Rejecting a true null is a Type I error, or false positive. Type II is failing to reject a false null.

questions.stem: A debate team increases sample size; what happens to the power of the test?
questions.explanation: Larger samples reduce standard error, increasing power. Power is not the p-value.

questions.stem: A debate team score is 85 with mean 70 and sd 5. Compute the z-score.
questions.explanation: z=(85-70)/5=3. Standardize by subtracting mean and dividing by sd.

questions.topic: The standard error of a mean
questions.learningObjective: Compute standard error of the mean
questions.stem: A debate team sample has sd 12 and n=36. Compute the standard error of the mean.
questions.explanation: SE=sd/sqrt(n)=12/6=2. Standard error decreases with sqrt(n).

questions.stem: A debate team reports a 95% CI for mean score is [60,70]. What does 95% refer to?

options.text: The sample mean equals the true mean 95% of the time
There is a 95% chance the true mean is in this interval
95% of scores fall in the interval
The method captures the true mean 95% of the time

questions.explanation: 95% describes the long-run capture rate of the method, not probability about this fixed interval. Frequentist interpretation.

questions.stem: A debate team gets p=0.03 for a null hypothesis. What does that mean?

options.text: Probability the null hypothesis is true
Probability of data this extreme if null true

questions.explanation: A p-value is the probability of observed or more extreme data assuming the null is true. It is not P(null true).

questions.stem: A debate team test has 99% accuracy and disease prevalence 1%. If positive, approximate P(disease)? Use Bayes: (0.99*0.01)/(0.99*0.01+0.01*0.99).
questions.explanation: Numerator 0.0099, denominator 0.0099+0.0099=0.0198, ratio 0.5. Base rate matters.

questions.stem: A debate team tests whether a new method improves scores. What is the null hypothesis?

options.text: The new method has no effect on scores

questions.explanation: The null states no effect or no difference; the alternative states improvement. Keep them distinct.

questions.learningObjective: Apply a decision rule with alpha
questions.stem: A debate team uses alpha=0.05 and gets p=0.04. What decision follows?

options.misconception: confuses fail to reject with accept

questions.explanation: When p <= alpha, reject the null. Do not accept the null; only fail to reject.

questions.stem: A debate team's residual plot shows a curved pattern. What does that suggest?

options.text: A nonlinear relationship may be needed

questions.explanation: A curved residual pattern indicates nonlinearity; the linear model misses structure. Independence and constant variance are separate checks.

questions.stem: A debate team plots data forming a U-shape. What kind of relationship is that?
questions.explanation: A U-shape indicates a nonlinear, often quadratic, relationship. Linear models would be inadequate.

questions.stem: A debate team's residual spread widens as x increases. What is this called?
questions.explanation: Widening spread indicates heteroscedasticity, violating constant variance. Homoscedasticity would show even spread.

questions.topic: What an analysis of variance tests
questions.stem: A debate team runs ANOVA on three groups. What does it test?

options.text: Whether all group variances are equal
Whether all group means are equal

questions.explanation: ANOVA tests equality of group means. Variance equality and normality are separate assumptions.

questions.topic: Slope of a line of best fit
questions.stem: A debate team's regression of score on hours has slope 2.5. What does that mean?

options.text: Scores increase by 2.5 total regardless of hours
Each extra hour associates with 2.5 more score points

questions.explanation: Slope is the change in response per unit change in predictor. It is not correlation or intercept.

questions.topic: Predictions from a line of best fit
questions.stem: A debate team's fit is y=2x+10. Predict y when x=4.
questions.explanation: Substitute x=4: 2*4+10=18. Use the fitted equation for prediction.

questions.stem: A debate team observes y=20 and the model predicts 17. Compute the residual.
questions.explanation: Residual = observed - predicted = 20-17=3. Sign indicates above or below fit.

questions.stem: A debate team has covariance 12, sd_x=3, sd_y=4. Compute r.
questions.explanation: r=cov/(sd_x*sd_y)=12/(3*4)=1. Correlation standardizes covariance.
questions.hint: Divide covariance by product of sd

questions.learningObjective: Compute expected count in a table
questions.stem: A debate team table has row total 50, column total 40, grand total 200. Compute expected count.
questions.explanation: Expected = (row total*column total)/grand total = 50*40/200=10. Expected counts assume independence.
questions.hint: Multiply totals and divide by grand

questions.stem: A debate team cell has observed 12 and expected 10. Compute (O-E)^2/E.
questions.explanation: (12-10)^2/10=4/10=0.4. Each cell contributes this quantity.

questions.topic: Updating a probability from a test result
questions.stem: A debate team updates P(disease) from 0.1 to posterior 0.5 after a positive test. What is the posterior probability?
questions.explanation: The posterior probability after the positive test is 0.5. Bayes updating combines prior with likelihood.

questions.stem: A debate team has binomial n=100, p=0.3. Compute the standard deviation of the count.
questions.explanation: sd=sqrt(np(1-p))=sqrt(100*0.3*0.7)=sqrt(21)=4.58. Binomial spread formula.

questions.stem: A debate team finds a statistically significant but tiny effect. What can we say?

options.text: No conclusion possible without effect size
Tiny effects are always practically important
Statistically significant does not imply practically important

questions.explanation: Statistical significance addresses sampling; practical significance addresses real-world importance. Both matter.

questions.topic: Why the null is the default
questions.stem: A debate team asks why the null hypothesis is the default. Explain in one or two sentences.

answer.exemplar: The null is the default because it represents no effect or status quo, requiring evidence to overturn; this controls false positives by placing the burden of proof on the claim.

questions.explanation: Defaulting to no effect controls false positives and sets a burden of proof. Evidence must overcome the null.

questions.stem: A debate team reports a 90% CI. Explain what that interval claims about the parameter.

answer.exemplar: A 90% confidence interval claims that the method used to construct it captures the true parameter in 90% of repeated samples, not that this particular interval has 90% probability.

questions.explanation: The interval claims method reliability, not probability about this interval. Frequentist framing.

questions.learningObjective: Count outcomes in a sample space
questions.stem: A debate team flips two coins. How many outcomes are in the sample space?
questions.explanation: Each coin has 2 outcomes, so 2*2=4 total. Multiply independent possibilities.

questions.stem: A debate team rolls a fair die. What is P(even)?
questions.explanation: Three even faces out of six gives 3/6=0.5. Count favorable over total.

questions.stem: A debate team spinner has P(red)=0.4 and P(blue)=0.6. What is P(not red)?
questions.explanation: Complement of red is blue with probability 0.6. Use complement rule.

questions.stem: A debate team chooses 2 from 5. Compute C(5,2).
questions.explanation: C(5,2)=5*4/2=10. Combination formula n!/(k!(n-k)!).

questions.stem: A debate team has P(A)=0.5, P(B)=0.4, P(A and B)=0.3. Are A and B independent?

options.text: Yes, because both probabilities are positive

questions.explanation: Independence requires P(A and B)=P(A)P(B); 0.3≠0.2, so dependent. Product check decides.

questions.stem: A debate team sees r=0.2 and r=0.9 in two studies. Which indicates stronger linear association?
questions.explanation: Larger absolute r means stronger linear association. Correlation is not slope.

questions.stem: A debate team notes stork populations and birth rates correlate; what is likely?

options.text: A confounding variable such as rural area

questions.explanation: A common confounder like rural area can create spurious correlation. Correlation alone proves nothing.

questions.stem: A debate team wants regression on color with no ordinal meaning. Which encoding is safer?
questions.explanation: One-hot avoids imposing false ordinal order on nominal categories. Label encoding can mislead regression.

questions.stem: A debate team samples volunteers online and concludes all adults agree. Find the error.

options.text: Volunteer online sample is not representative

questions.explanation: Volunteer online samples suffer selection bias, so generalization is unsupported. Bias, not just p-values, matters.

questions.stem: A debate team's t-test assumes normality. Is this fully verifiable with small samples?

options.text: Yes, by the central limit theorem
Yes, by a normality test always
No, small samples give limited evidence

questions.explanation: Small samples provide limited evidence for normality; tests have low power. CLT helps for large n.

questions.stem: A debate team tree: P(rain)=0.4, P(win|rain)=0.5, P(win|no rain)=0.7. Compute P(win).
questions.explanation: P(win)=0.4*0.5+0.6*0.7=0.2+0.42=0.62. Law of total probability.

questions.stem: A debate team has P(A)=0.3, P(B)=0.5, P(A and B)=0.15. Compute P(B|A).
questions.explanation: P(B|A)=0.15/0.3=0.5. Condition on A by dividing.

questions.stem: A debate team has 4 independent questions with p=0.5. What is P(exactly 2 correct)?
questions.explanation: C(4,2)*(0.5)^2*(0.5)^2=6*0.0625=0.375. Binomial probability formula.

questions.learningObjective: Apply empirical rule to two sd
questions.stem: A debate team's normal scores have mean 60 and sd 8. About what percent are within two sd of the mean?
questions.explanation: Empirical rule gives about 95% within two standard deviations. Classic 68-95-99.7.

questions.topic: Normal distributions and the empirical rule
questions.stem: A debate team's normal scores have mean 50 and sd 10. About what percent are below 30?
questions.explanation: 30 is two sd below mean; lower tail beyond two sd is about 2.5%. Empirical rule.

questions.stem: A debate team population mean is 70. What is the mean of the sampling distribution of the sample mean?
questions.explanation: The sampling distribution of the sample mean is centered at the population mean, 70. Unbiasedness.

questions.topic: Type one and type two errors
questions.stem: A debate team fails to reject a false null. Which error is that?

options.text: Type I error, a false positive
Type II error, a false negative

questions.explanation: Failing to reject a false null is Type II error, a false negative. Type I is false positive.
questions.hint: Fail to reject false null = Type II

questions.learningObjective: Relate power to Type II error
questions.stem: A debate team increases alpha. What happens to power and Type II error?

options.text: Power decreases and Type II error increases
Power increases and Type II error decreases

questions.explanation: Higher alpha increases power and decreases Type II error, trading off Type I. Tradeoff relationship.

questions.stem: A debate team sample mean is 72, population mean 70, SE 2. Compute z-score.
questions.explanation: z=(72-70)/2=1. Standardize sample mean by SE.

questions.topic: The standard error of a mean
questions.stem: A debate team sample has sd 9 and n=81. Compute the standard error of the mean.
questions.explanation: SE=9/sqrt(81)=9/9=1. Larger n reduces SE.
